name: Leg Swings (Front-to-Back)
instructions: Stand next to a wall or sturdy support, holding on lightly for balance.
Swing one leg forward and backward in a controlled, pendulum-like motion, keeping the knee slightly soft.
Perform the desired number of swings, then switch legs.
coachNote: A classic pre-run and pre-lower-body-session warm-up that dynamically opens the hip through its sagittal range before loaded movement.
tips: Keep the swing controlled rather than using momentum to force extra range.
Keep the torso upright throughout.
commonMistakes: Swinging too aggressively and losing control.
Rounding the back to compensate for limited hip range.
benefits: Dynamically warms up the hip flexors and hamstrings.
Prepares the hips for running or lower-body training.
safetyNotes: Hold a stable support for balance.
Start with a small range and gradually increase.
startingPosition: Standing, holding a support, one leg free to swing.
endingPosition: Same position, leg swung through its range repeatedly.

name: Leg Swings (Lateral)
instructions: Stand facing a wall or sturdy support, holding on with both hands.
Swing one leg across your body and out to the side in a controlled, pendulum-like motion.
Perform the desired number of swings, then switch legs.
coachNote: Complements the front-to-back leg swing by opening the hip through the frontal plane, important for lateral movements and squatting mechanics.
tips: Keep the hips facing forward throughout the swing.
Increase range gradually rather than forcing it.
commonMistakes: Rotating the hips instead of keeping them square.
Using momentum excessively instead of controlled range.
benefits: Dynamically warms up the adductors and abductors.
Improves lateral hip mobility for squatting and lunging.
safetyNotes: Hold a stable support for balance.
Start with a small range and gradually increase.
startingPosition: Standing, facing a support, one leg free to swing.
endingPosition: Same position, leg swung through its range repeatedly.

name: Arm Circles
instructions: Stand tall with arms extended out to your sides at shoulder height.
Make small circles with your arms, gradually increasing the circle size for the first half of the set.
Reverse direction for the second half of the set.
coachNote: A simple, universally used shoulder warm-up before any upper-body pressing, pulling, or overhead work.
tips: Start with small circles and progressively increase size.
Keep the shoulders down away from the ears.
commonMistakes: Starting with circles too large before warming up.
Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears.
benefits: Warms up the shoulder joint through its full range.
Quick and requires no equipment.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement controlled and pain-free.
Start small and build range gradually.
startingPosition: Standing, arms extended to the sides.
endingPosition: Same position, arms circling continuously.

name: Walking Lunge with Twist
instructions: Step forward into a lunge, lowering the back knee toward the ground.
Rotate your torso toward the front leg, reaching both arms with the twist.
Return to center, step through into the next lunge on the opposite leg, and repeat while walking forward.
coachNote: Combines hip flexor stretching with thoracic rotation, making it an efficient full-body dynamic warm-up before squatting or rotational sports.
tips: Keep the front knee tracking over the foot.
Rotate from the torso, not just the arms.
commonMistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward.
Rotating the hips instead of just the torso.
benefits: Combines hip and thoracic mobility in one movement.
Excellent dynamic full-body warm-up.
safetyNotes: Use a controlled lunge depth appropriate to your mobility.
Keep the movement smooth rather than bouncing.
startingPosition: Standing, about to step into a lunge.
endingPosition: Lunge position, torso rotated toward the front leg.

name: Inchworm Walkout
instructions: Stand tall, then hinge at the hips and place your hands on the floor.
Walk your hands forward into a high plank position, keeping the legs as straight as comfortable.
Walk your feet forward toward your hands, then stand back up and repeat.
coachNote: A full-body dynamic warm-up that stretches the posterior chain while also activating the shoulders and core through the plank phase.
tips: Keep the legs as straight as possible without forcing pain.
Keep the core braced during the plank phase.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees excessively to avoid the hamstring stretch.
Letting the hips sag during the plank phase.
benefits: Combines hamstring flexibility with core and shoulder activation.
Excellent full-body dynamic warm-up.
safetyNotes: Allow a slight knee bend if hamstring flexibility is limited.
Keep the wrists aligned under the shoulders during the plank.
startingPosition: Standing tall.
endingPosition: High plank position after walking the hands out.

name: World's Greatest Stretch
instructions: Step into a deep lunge, placing both hands on the ground inside the front foot.
Rotate your torso and reach the same-side arm toward the ceiling, opening your chest toward the front leg.
Return the hand to the ground, then straighten the front leg to stretch the hamstring, and repeat the sequence before switching legs.
coachNote: Aptly named for hitting the hip flexors, hamstrings, adductors, and thoracic spine all in a single flowing sequence, making it a go-to comprehensive warm-up.
tips: Move through each position with control rather than rushing.
Keep the back leg's knee extended and glute engaged.
commonMistakes: Rushing through the sequence without holding each position briefly.
Letting the front knee cave inward during the rotation.
benefits: Addresses multiple major mobility restrictions in one flowing sequence.
Excellent comprehensive pre-workout warm-up.
safetyNotes: Move within a pain-free range throughout.
Warm up gently before attempting deeper positions.
startingPosition: Deep lunge, hands on the ground inside the front foot.
endingPosition: Torso rotated, arm reaching toward the ceiling.

name: Hip Circles (Standing)
instructions: Stand on one leg, holding a support if needed, with the other knee lifted to hip height.
Circle the lifted knee outward, around, and back to the starting position in a controlled motion.
Perform the desired number of circles, then reverse direction and switch legs.
coachNote: Opens the hip capsule through a full circular range, useful as a warm-up before squats, lunges, or any lower-body training.
tips: Keep the standing leg stable and the core braced.
Make the circles as large as comfortable without pain.
commonMistakes: Losing balance and rushing the movement.
Making circles too small to provide real benefit.
benefits: Opens the hip through its full range of motion.
Improves balance alongside hip mobility.
safetyNotes: Hold a support if balance is a concern.
Move within a pain-free range.
startingPosition: Standing on one leg, other knee lifted.
endingPosition: Same position, knee circling continuously.

name: Cat-Cow Stretch
instructions: Start on hands and knees in a tabletop position, wrists under shoulders and knees under hips.
Inhale, arch your back and lift your chest and tailbone toward the ceiling (cow position).
Exhale, round your spine toward the ceiling, tucking your chin and tailbone (cat position), and continue alternating.
coachNote: One of the most fundamental spinal mobility drills, commonly used to warm up the spine before training or to relieve stiffness after sitting.
tips: Move slowly and coordinate the movement with your breathing.
Move through the entire length of the spine, not just the lower back.
commonMistakes: Moving too quickly without controlling each phase.
Only moving the lower back instead of the full spine.
benefits: Improves spinal mobility through flexion and extension.
Relieves tension from prolonged sitting.
safetyNotes: Move within a pain-free range.
Use a mat for knee comfort.
startingPosition: Tabletop position on hands and knees.
endingPosition: Same position, alternating between arched and rounded spine.

name: Scorpion Stretch
instructions: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended out to the sides at shoulder height.
Lift one leg and rotate your hips to reach that foot across your body toward the opposite hand.
Return to the starting position and repeat on the other side, alternating continuously.
coachNote: Dynamically opens the hips and lower back through rotation, commonly used in athletic and running warm-up routines.
tips: Keep both shoulders on the ground as you rotate.
Move through a controlled, pain-free range.
commonMistakes: Lifting the shoulder off the ground to reach further.
Forcing the range beyond comfortable limits.
benefits: Opens the hips and lower back through rotation.
Effective dynamic warm-up for running and rotational sports.
safetyNotes: Move within a pain-free range, especially for the lower back.
Warm up gently before increasing range.
startingPosition: Lying face down, arms extended to the sides.
endingPosition: One leg rotated across the body toward the opposite hand.

name: Frankenstein Walk
instructions: Stand tall with arms extended straight out in front at shoulder height.
Walk forward, kicking one straight leg up to meet the opposite hand with each step.
Continue alternating legs while walking forward for the desired distance or reps.
coachNote: A dynamic hamstring stretch performed while walking, ideal as part of a pre-run or pre-sprint warm-up routine.
tips: Keep the kicking leg as straight as comfortable.
Keep the torso tall rather than leaning back excessively.
commonMistakes: Leaning back too far to compensate for tight hamstrings.
Kicking with a bent knee instead of a straight leg.
benefits: Dynamically stretches the hamstrings while warming up locomotion.
No equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Move within a pain-free range.
Keep the standing leg stable with each step.
startingPosition: Standing, arms extended forward.
endingPosition: One leg kicked up to meet the opposite hand.

name: Standing Hamstring Stretch
instructions: Stand tall and place one heel on a low surface in front of you, leg straight.
Hinge forward at the hips, keeping your back flat, until you feel a stretch in the back of the raised leg.
Hold the stretch for the prescribed duration, then switch legs.
coachNote: A simple, widely accessible static stretch for the hamstrings, best performed after training when the muscles are warm.
tips: Hinge from the hips, keeping the back flat rather than rounding.
Hold the stretch without bouncing.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back to reach further forward.
Bouncing instead of holding a steady stretch.
benefits: Improves hamstring flexibility.
Simple to perform with any elevated surface.
safetyNotes: Stretch only to mild tension, not pain.
Perform after a light warm-up for best results.
startingPosition: Standing, heel of one leg on an elevated surface.
endingPosition: Torso hinged forward over the raised leg.

name: Seated Hamstring Stretch
instructions: Sit on the floor with one leg extended straight and the other bent, foot resting against the inner thigh.
Hinge forward at the hips over the straight leg, reaching toward your foot while keeping the back flat.
Hold the stretch for the prescribed duration, then switch legs.
coachNote: A staple cool-down stretch that isolates one hamstring at a time, allowing a deeper, more controlled stretch than bilateral versions.
tips: Hinge from the hips rather than rounding the upper back.
Keep the extended leg's knee straight but not locked forcefully.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back to reach further.
Bouncing instead of holding steady.
benefits: Allows a deep, isolated hamstring stretch.
Simple, equipment-free cool-down option.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Sit on a cushioned surface for comfort.
startingPosition: Seated, one leg extended, one bent.
endingPosition: Torso hinged forward over the extended leg.

name: Standing Quad Stretch
instructions: Stand tall, holding a support for balance if needed.
Bend one knee, bringing your heel toward your glutes, and grasp your ankle or foot with the same-side hand.
Gently pull the heel closer while keeping your knees aligned, and hold the stretch before switching legs.
coachNote: A go-to post-run or post-leg-day stretch for the quadriceps, best done standing to also lightly engage the hip flexors.
tips: Keep the knees close together throughout the stretch.
Keep the standing leg's knee slightly soft, not locked.
commonMistakes: Letting the bent knee drift out to the side.
Arching the lower back excessively to increase the stretch.
benefits: Improves quadriceps and hip flexor flexibility.
Simple and equipment-free.
safetyNotes: Hold a support if balance is a concern.
Stretch to mild tension only.
startingPosition: Standing, one knee bent, foot held behind you.
endingPosition: Same position, heel pulled toward the glutes.

name: Couch Stretch
instructions: Kneel in front of a wall or couch, placing the top of your back foot up against it with the knee bent.
Bring your front foot forward into a lunge position, keeping your torso upright.
Gently press your hips forward until you feel a deep stretch in the hip flexor and quad of the back leg, and hold.
coachNote: A deep, highly effective hip flexor stretch popularized in mobility training circles for its ability to target a commonly tight muscle group thoroughly.
tips: Keep the torso upright rather than leaning forward.
Squeeze the glute of the back leg to deepen the stretch safely.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back excessively instead of squeezing the glute.
Progressing to the full position too quickly before building tolerance.
benefits: Provides one of the deepest available hip flexor stretches.
Effective for counteracting prolonged sitting.
safetyNotes: Use a cushion under the back knee for comfort.
Build up the depth of the stretch gradually over sessions.
startingPosition: Kneeling, back foot against a wall, knee bent.
endingPosition: Hips pressed forward, front leg lunged.

name: Butterfly Stretch
instructions: Sit on the floor with the soles of your feet pressed together, knees bent out to the sides.
Hold your feet or ankles and gently press your knees toward the ground using your elbows or hip muscles.
Hold the stretch for the prescribed duration, breathing steadily.
coachNote: A classic seated stretch for the inner thighs, commonly used in yoga and general flexibility routines to prepare for wider-stance lower-body work.
tips: Keep the back straight rather than rounding forward excessively.
Press the knees down gently rather than forcing them.
commonMistakes: Bouncing the knees instead of holding a steady stretch.
Rounding the back significantly to lean forward.
benefits: Improves adductor and groin flexibility.
Simple, accessible seated stretch.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Sit on a cushioned surface for comfort.
startingPosition: Seated, soles of the feet together, knees out.
endingPosition: Same position, knees pressed gently toward the floor.

name: Pigeon Pose Stretch
instructions: From a tabletop position, bring one knee forward and place it behind your same-side wrist, shin angled across the body.
Extend the opposite leg straight back behind you, hips squared toward the floor.
Lower your torso forward over the bent leg and hold the stretch, then switch sides.
coachNote: A deep hip external rotator and glute stretch commonly used in yoga practice, particularly effective for runners and lifters with tight hips.
tips: Keep the hips as square to the floor as possible.
Use a cushion under the hip if needed for comfort.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rotate open instead of staying squared.
Forcing the front shin into a position beyond comfortable range.
benefits: Provides a deep stretch for the glutes and hip rotators.
Popular and effective for runners and athletes with tight hips.
safetyNotes: Move into the position gradually, avoiding knee pain.
Use padding under the hips and knees for comfort.
startingPosition: Tabletop position, transitioning into the pigeon shape.
endingPosition: Torso lowered forward over the bent front leg.

name: Figure-4 Stretch
instructions: Lie on your back with both knees bent, feet flat on the floor.
Cross one ankle over the opposite knee, forming a figure-4 shape.
Reach through and grasp the back of the uncrossed leg's thigh, gently pulling it toward your chest until you feel a stretch in the crossed leg's glute.
coachNote: A gentler, more accessible alternative to pigeon pose for stretching the glutes and piriformis, easy to perform on the floor or in bed.
tips: Keep the head and shoulders relaxed on the ground.
Pull gently rather than forcing the stretch.
commonMistakes: Pulling too hard and causing discomfort in the knee.
Lifting the head and shoulders off the ground unnecessarily.
benefits: Accessible, low-impact way to stretch the glutes.
Can be done nearly anywhere with just a floor.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Support the head with a cushion if desired.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, knees bent, ankle crossed over the opposite knee.
endingPosition: Uncrossed leg pulled toward the chest.

name: Wall Calf Stretch
instructions: Stand facing a wall, placing your hands on it at shoulder height.
Step one foot back, keeping the back leg straight and the heel pressed into the floor.
Lean your hips toward the wall until you feel a stretch in the back leg's calf, and hold before switching legs.
coachNote: A fundamental stretch for the gastrocnemius, useful for runners and anyone recovering from calf tightness or ankle stiffness.
tips: Keep the back heel pressed firmly into the floor.
Keep the back leg's knee straight for a gastrocnemius-focused stretch, or bend it slightly to target the soleus.
commonMistakes: Letting the back heel lift off the ground.
Turning the back foot outward instead of pointing it forward.
benefits: Improves calf and ankle flexibility.
Simple to perform against any wall.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Keep the front knee soft, not locked.
startingPosition: Standing, hands on the wall, one foot stepped back.
endingPosition: Hips leaned toward the wall, back leg's calf stretched.

name: Standing IT Band Stretch
instructions: Stand tall and cross one leg behind the other.
Lean your torso and hips to the side of the back leg, reaching the same-side arm overhead.
Hold the stretch, feeling it along the outside of the back leg's hip and thigh, then switch sides.
coachNote: Targets the notoriously stubborn IT band and lateral hip, useful for runners and cyclists dealing with lateral knee or hip discomfort.
tips: Keep both feet flat on the ground throughout.
Reach the arm overhead to deepen the side stretch.
commonMistakes: Bending forward instead of leaning purely to the side.
Losing balance and stepping out of position.
benefits: Targets the lateral hip and IT band region.
Simple and equipment-free.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Use a wall for balance support if needed.
startingPosition: Standing, one leg crossed behind the other.
endingPosition: Torso leaned to the side, arm reaching overhead.

name: Frog Stretch
instructions: Start on hands and knees, then widen your knees out as far as comfortable, keeping ankles in line with the knees.
Lower your hips back and down toward your heels, resting on your forearms if needed.
Hold the stretch, feeling it deeply in the inner thighs, breathing steadily throughout.
coachNote: A deep adductor stretch popular among athletes needing significant hip mobility, such as those in martial arts, gymnastics, or Olympic weightlifting.
tips: Widen the knees only as far as comfortable without pain.
Keep the ankles in line with the knees to protect the knee joint.
commonMistakes: Widening the knees too aggressively before building tolerance.
Letting the ankles splay outward beyond the knees.
benefits: Provides one of the deepest available adductor stretches.
Useful for athletes needing extensive hip mobility.
safetyNotes: Progress the depth of this stretch gradually over time.
Use a cushioned surface for the knees.
startingPosition: On hands and knees, knees widened out.
endingPosition: Hips lowered back and down, forearms on the ground.

name: Side Lunge Adductor Stretch
instructions: Stand with feet wide apart, toes pointing forward.
Shift your weight to one side, bending that knee while keeping the opposite leg straight, feeling a stretch along its inner thigh.
Hold the stretch, then shift to the other side and repeat.
coachNote: A standing alternative to the butterfly or frog stretch, useful as part of a dynamic-to-static transition before or after lower-body training.
tips: Keep the straight leg's foot flat on the ground.
Keep the bent knee tracking over the toes.
commonMistakes: Letting the straight leg's heel lift off the ground.
Leaning the torso too far forward.
benefits: Improves adductor flexibility in a standing position.
Easy to transition into from a standing warm-up.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Keep the stance stable throughout.
startingPosition: Standing, feet wide apart.
endingPosition: Weight shifted to one side, opposite leg straight.

name: 90/90 Hip Stretch
instructions: Sit on the floor with the front leg bent at 90 degrees in front of you and the back leg bent at 90 degrees behind you.
Keep your torso upright and both sit bones on the ground, feeling a stretch in the hips of both legs.
Hold the position, optionally leaning forward over the front leg to deepen the stretch, then switch sides.
coachNote: A comprehensive hip stretch that targets internal and external rotation simultaneously, widely used in modern mobility training programs.
tips: Keep both sit bones grounded rather than leaning to one side.
Keep the front shin as close to perpendicular to the body as comfortable.
commonMistakes: Leaning heavily to one side to compensate for tight hips.
Forcing the shins into a 90-degree angle before it's comfortable.
benefits: Targets both internal and external hip rotation.
Comprehensive hip mobility stretch used widely in modern training.
safetyNotes: Move into the position gradually.
Use a cushion under the hips if needed.
startingPosition: Seated, front leg and back leg both bent at 90 degrees.
endingPosition: Torso upright or leaned forward over the front leg.

name: Cross-Body Shoulder Stretch
instructions: Stand or sit tall and bring one arm straight across your chest.
Use your opposite hand or forearm to gently pull the extended arm closer to your body.
Hold the stretch, feeling it in the back of the shoulder, then switch arms.
coachNote: A simple, effective stretch for the posterior deltoid, commonly used after pressing or overhead work to relieve shoulder tension.
tips: Keep the shoulder of the stretching arm relaxed and down.
Pull gently rather than forcing the stretch.
commonMistakes: Shrugging the shoulder up during the stretch.
Pulling too aggressively, causing discomfort.
benefits: Relieves tension in the posterior shoulder.
Quick and easy to perform anywhere.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Avoid this stretch if experiencing acute shoulder pain.
startingPosition: Standing, one arm extended across the chest.
endingPosition: Arm pulled closer to the body with the opposite hand.

name: Overhead Triceps Stretch
instructions: Stand or sit tall and raise one arm overhead, bending the elbow to reach your hand down your back.
Use your opposite hand to gently press on the raised elbow, deepening the stretch.
Hold the stretch, feeling it along the back of the arm, then switch sides.
coachNote: A standard post-pressing cool-down stretch that also mildly stretches the lat, useful for relieving overhead-work-related tightness.
tips: Keep the torso tall rather than leaning to the side.
Press gently on the elbow rather than forcing it.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back to compensate for shoulder tightness.
Pressing too aggressively on the elbow.
benefits: Stretches the triceps and lat together.
Simple and equipment-free.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Avoid if experiencing acute elbow or shoulder pain.
startingPosition: Standing, one arm raised overhead and bent behind the head.
endingPosition: Opposite hand pressing gently on the raised elbow.

name: Doorway Chest Stretch
instructions: Stand in a doorway, placing your forearms on each side of the frame with elbows bent around 90 degrees.
Step one foot forward through the doorway, leaning your body weight forward until you feel a stretch across your chest.
Hold the stretch, then step back to release.
coachNote: A highly effective counter-stretch for the anterior chest and shoulders, especially important for those who spend long hours at a desk or do heavy pressing work.
tips: Keep the elbows roughly in line with the shoulders.
Lean forward gradually rather than lunging in aggressively.
commonMistakes: Setting the arms too high or low relative to the shoulders.
Leaning in too aggressively, causing shoulder discomfort.
benefits: Effectively counters tightness from pressing exercises and desk posture.
Easy to perform using any standard doorway.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Avoid if experiencing acute shoulder pain.
startingPosition: Standing in a doorway, forearms on the frame.
endingPosition: Body leaned forward through the doorway.

name: Lat Side-Bend Stretch
instructions: Stand tall and raise one arm overhead, clasping your hands together if desired.
Lean your torso to the opposite side, feeling a stretch along the side of your body and the raised arm's lat.
Hold the stretch, then switch sides.
coachNote: Useful after pulling exercises or overhead work to relieve tension through the lats and obliques together.
tips: Keep the hips square and facing forward.
Lean directly to the side rather than rotating forward.
commonMistakes: Rotating the torso instead of bending purely laterally.
Leaning forward instead of directly sideways.
benefits: Stretches the lats and obliques together.
Simple and equipment-free.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Keep the movement controlled without bouncing.
startingPosition: Standing, one arm raised overhead.
endingPosition: Torso leaned to the opposite side.

name: Neck Lateral Stretch
instructions: Sit or stand tall, then gently tilt your head to one side, bringing your ear toward your shoulder.
Optionally, use the same-side hand to apply very light additional pressure.
Hold the stretch, then return to center and repeat on the other side.
coachNote: A gentle, accessible stretch for relieving neck and upper trapezius tension from stress or prolonged screen use.
tips: Keep the shoulder of the stretching side relaxed and down.
Apply only very light pressure with the hand if used.
commonMistakes: Applying too much pressure with the hand.
Shrugging the opposite shoulder up during the stretch.
benefits: Relieves neck and upper trapezius tension.
Quick and accessible anywhere.
safetyNotes: Use very gentle pressure given the sensitivity of the neck.
Avoid this stretch if experiencing acute neck pain or injury.
startingPosition: Sitting or standing tall.
endingPosition: Head tilted to one side, ear toward the shoulder.

name: Neck Rotation Stretch
instructions: Sit or stand tall, then gently turn your head to look over one shoulder.
Hold the position at a comfortable end range, feeling a mild stretch along the side of the neck.
Return to center and repeat on the other side.
coachNote: Complements the lateral neck stretch by targeting rotational tightness, useful for those with stiffness from desk work or driving.
tips: Turn only to a comfortable range without forcing it.
Keep the shoulders relaxed and level throughout.
commonMistakes: Forcing the rotation beyond a comfortable range.
Lifting the shoulder on the side being stretched.
benefits: Improves neck rotational mobility.
Quick and accessible anywhere.
safetyNotes: Move gently given the sensitivity of the neck.
Avoid this stretch if experiencing acute neck pain or injury.
startingPosition: Sitting or standing tall.
endingPosition: Head turned to look over one shoulder.

name: Wrist Flexor Stretch
instructions: Extend one arm in front of you, palm facing up.
Use your opposite hand to gently pull the fingers of the extended hand down and back toward your body.
Hold the stretch, feeling it along the inside of the forearm, then switch arms.
coachNote: Important for lifters who perform significant gripping or curling work, and useful for relieving forearm tightness from typing.
tips: Keep the extended arm's elbow straight but not locked forcefully.
Pull gently rather than forcing the stretch.
commonMistakes: Pulling too aggressively, risking wrist strain.
Bending the elbow, reducing the stretch effectiveness.
benefits: Relieves forearm and wrist flexor tightness.
Useful after heavy gripping or curling exercises.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Avoid if experiencing acute wrist pain.
startingPosition: Arm extended, palm facing up.
endingPosition: Fingers pulled down and back with the opposite hand.

name: Wrist Extensor Stretch
instructions: Extend one arm in front of you, palm facing down, and let the hand relax downward at the wrist.
Use your opposite hand to gently press the back of the extended hand, deepening the stretch.
Hold the stretch, feeling it along the top of the forearm, then switch arms.
coachNote: Complements the wrist flexor stretch, important for lifters doing heavy pressing work where the wrist extensors work hard to stabilize the joint.
tips: Keep the extended arm's elbow straight but not locked forcefully.
Press gently rather than forcing the stretch.
commonMistakes: Pressing too aggressively, risking wrist strain.
Bending the elbow, reducing the stretch effectiveness.
benefits: Relieves forearm and wrist extensor tightness.
Useful after heavy pressing or gripping exercises.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Avoid if experiencing acute wrist pain.
startingPosition: Arm extended, palm facing down.
endingPosition: Back of the hand pressed with the opposite hand.

name: Wall Bicep Stretch
instructions: Stand next to a wall and place one arm straight behind you, palm flat against the wall at about hip height.
Gently rotate your torso away from the wall until you feel a stretch along the front of your arm and shoulder.
Hold the stretch, then switch arms.
coachNote: A useful counter-stretch after heavy curling or pulling work, since the biceps rarely get direct attention in typical stretching routines.
tips: Keep the arm straight throughout the stretch.
Rotate the torso gradually rather than jerking into position.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbow, reducing the stretch effectiveness.
Rotating too aggressively, risking shoulder strain.
benefits: Provides a targeted biceps stretch, rarely addressed elsewhere.
Simple to perform against any wall.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Avoid if experiencing acute shoulder or elbow pain.
startingPosition: Standing beside a wall, arm behind you, palm on the wall.
endingPosition: Torso rotated away from the wall.

name: Upper Trapezius Stretch
instructions: Sit or stand tall, gripping the seat or letting one arm hang at your side.
Tilt your head away from the anchored arm and slightly forward, feeling a stretch along the top of the shoulder and neck.
Hold the stretch, then switch sides.
coachNote: Specifically targets the upper trapezius, a muscle that carries significant tension from stress, shrugging, and desk posture.
tips: Anchor the arm to increase the stretch depth safely.
Tilt the head gently rather than forcing the range.
commonMistakes: Forcing the head into position too aggressively.
Not anchoring the arm, reducing the stretch's effectiveness.
benefits: Directly targets the upper trapezius, a common area of tension.
Quick and accessible anywhere.
safetyNotes: Use very gentle pressure given the sensitivity of the neck.
Avoid this stretch if experiencing acute neck pain.
startingPosition: Sitting or standing, one arm anchored down.
endingPosition: Head tilted away from the anchored arm.

name: Foam Roll Quadriceps
instructions: Lie face down with the foam roller positioned under your thighs, supporting your upper body on your forearms.
Roll slowly from just above the knee up to just below the hip, pausing on any tender spots.
Continue for the desired duration, then switch legs or roll both together.
coachNote: Regular foam rolling of the quads before training can help improve short-term range of motion and reduce the sensation of muscle tightness.
tips: Roll slowly rather than quickly back and forth.
Pause and breathe on any particularly tender areas.
commonMistakes: Rolling directly over the kneecap.
Rolling too quickly to have any real effect.
benefits: May reduce muscle tightness and improve short-term flexibility.
Simple self-administered recovery tool.
safetyNotes: Avoid rolling directly over joints or bones.
Avoid rolling over acutely injured tissue.
startingPosition: Face down, foam roller under the thighs.
endingPosition: Same position, rolled along the length of the quads.

name: Foam Roll Hamstrings
instructions: Sit on the floor with the foam roller positioned under your thighs, hands placed behind you for support.
Roll slowly from just above the knee up to just below the glutes, pausing on any tender spots.
Continue for the desired duration, then switch legs or roll both together.
coachNote: A common pre- or post-leg-day recovery practice, often paired with active hamstring stretching for a fuller effect.
tips: Roll slowly rather than quickly back and forth.
Cross one leg over the other to increase pressure if desired.
commonMistakes: Rolling directly over the back of the knee.
Rolling too quickly to have any real effect.
benefits: May reduce muscle tightness and improve short-term flexibility.
Simple self-administered recovery tool.
safetyNotes: Avoid rolling directly over joints.
Avoid rolling over acutely injured tissue.
startingPosition: Seated, foam roller under the thighs.
endingPosition: Same position, rolled along the length of the hamstrings.

name: Foam Roll IT Band
instructions: Lie on your side with the foam roller positioned under the outside of your thigh, supporting yourself on your forearm.
Roll slowly from just above the knee up to just below the hip along the outside of the thigh.
Continue for the desired duration, then switch sides.
coachNote: Often reported as one of the more uncomfortable areas to foam roll due to the dense fascia, so starting with lighter pressure is recommended.
tips: Start with lighter pressure by keeping more weight on your other leg.
Roll slowly and pause on tender spots.
commonMistakes: Applying too much pressure too quickly before building tolerance.
Rolling too fast to have any real effect.
benefits: May reduce perceived tightness along the lateral thigh.
Simple self-administered recovery tool.
safetyNotes: Start with lighter pressure and build up gradually.
Avoid rolling directly over the knee joint.
startingPosition: Lying on the side, foam roller under the outer thigh.
endingPosition: Same position, rolled along the length of the IT band.

name: Foam Roll Upper Back
instructions: Lie on your back with the foam roller positioned horizontally under your upper back, knees bent, feet flat on the floor.
Support your head with your hands and gently roll from the base of your shoulder blades up to your upper back.
You may also pause and extend gently over the roller at a fixed point to mobilize the thoracic spine.
coachNote: Helps improve thoracic extension, which is often limited by prolonged sitting and can negatively affect overhead lifting and posture.
tips: Support your head throughout to protect the neck.
Move slowly and avoid rolling directly over the lower back.
commonMistakes: Rolling down into the lower back, which should not be rolled this way.
Not supporting the head, straining the neck.
benefits: Improves thoracic spine extension and mobility.
Helpful for counteracting rounded, seated posture.
safetyNotes: Do not roll directly over the lower back or neck.
Move slowly and within a comfortable range.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, foam roller under the upper back.
endingPosition: Same position, rolled or extended over the upper back.

name: Foam Roll Calves
instructions: Sit on the floor with the foam roller positioned under your calves, hands placed behind you for support.
Roll slowly from just above the ankle up to just below the knee, pausing on any tender spots.
Continue for the desired duration, then switch legs or roll both together.
coachNote: A quick, effective recovery practice for runners and lifters who accumulate significant calf tightness from training volume.
tips: Roll slowly rather than quickly back and forth.
Cross one leg over the other to increase pressure if desired.
commonMistakes: Rolling directly over the ankle joint.
Rolling too quickly to have any real effect.
benefits: May reduce muscle tightness and improve short-term flexibility.
Simple self-administered recovery tool.
safetyNotes: Avoid rolling directly over joints.
Avoid rolling over acutely injured tissue.
startingPosition: Seated, foam roller under the calves.
endingPosition: Same position, rolled along the length of the calves.

name: Foam Roll Glutes
instructions: Sit on the foam roller with one ankle crossed over the opposite knee, leaning slightly toward the crossed side.
Roll slowly over the glute of the crossed leg, pausing on any tender spots.
Continue for the desired duration, then switch sides.
coachNote: Especially useful before lower-body training to help reduce the sensation of glute and hip tightness before squatting or hinging patterns.
tips: Lean your weight to increase or decrease pressure as needed.
Roll slowly and pause on tender spots.
commonMistakes: Applying too much pressure too quickly.
Rolling too fast to have any real effect.
benefits: May reduce perceived glute and hip tightness.
Simple self-administered recovery tool.
safetyNotes: Start with lighter pressure and build up gradually.
Avoid rolling directly over the tailbone.
startingPosition: Seated on the foam roller, ankle crossed over the knee.
endingPosition: Same position, rolled over the glute.

name: Lacrosse Ball Glute Release
instructions: Sit on the floor and place a lacrosse ball under one side of your glutes.
Lean into the ball, adjusting your position to find a tender spot, and hold or make small movements over it.
Continue for the desired duration, then switch sides.
coachNote: The smaller, firmer ball allows for much more targeted pressure than a foam roller, useful for pinpointing specific tight spots deep in the glute.
tips: Start with lighter body weight on the ball and increase gradually.
Breathe steadily and relax into the pressure.
commonMistakes: Applying too much pressure too quickly before building tolerance.
Rolling directly over bony landmarks.
benefits: Provides targeted, precise pressure for deep tissue release.
Portable and inexpensive tool.
safetyNotes: Start with lighter pressure and build up gradually.
Avoid use over acutely injured or inflamed tissue.
startingPosition: Seated, lacrosse ball under one side of the glutes.
endingPosition: Same position, weight settled into the ball.

name: Lacrosse Ball Pec Release
instructions: Stand facing a wall and place a lacrosse ball between the wall and your chest muscle, near the front of the shoulder.
Lean your body weight into the ball, adjusting position to find a tender spot, and hold or make small circular movements.
Continue for the desired duration, then switch sides.
coachNote: Targets the pec minor and anterior shoulder, an area difficult to reach with a foam roller, often tight from pressing exercises and rounded posture.
tips: Start with lighter pressure by leaning less into the wall.
Avoid rolling directly over the collarbone.
commonMistakes: Applying too much pressure too quickly.
Positioning the ball directly over the collarbone or joint.
benefits: Provides targeted release for a hard-to-reach area.
Portable and inexpensive tool.
safetyNotes: Start with lighter pressure and build up gradually.
Avoid use over acutely injured or inflamed tissue.
startingPosition: Standing, lacrosse ball between the wall and chest.
endingPosition: Same position, weight leaned into the ball.

name: Downward Facing Dog
instructions: Start on hands and knees, then tuck your toes and lift your hips up and back, forming an inverted V-shape with your body.
Press your heels toward the floor and your chest toward your thighs, keeping arms and legs long.
Hold the position, breathing steadily, pedaling the heels gently if desired.
coachNote: One of the most recognizable yoga poses, offering a full posterior chain stretch alongside shoulder and upper back engagement.
tips: Bend the knees slightly if the hamstrings are tight to keep the spine straight.
Press firmly through the hands to lengthen the spine.
commonMistakes: Rounding the spine to force the heels down.
Placing the hands too close to the feet, limiting the stretch.
benefits: Stretches the entire posterior chain and shoulders.
Improves overall body awareness and breath control.
safetyNotes: Avoid if experiencing acute wrist pain.
Bend the knees as needed to protect the lower back.
startingPosition: Hands and knees, transitioning to an inverted V-shape.
endingPosition: Hips lifted high, heels reaching toward the floor.

name: Cobra Pose
instructions: Lie face down with your hands placed under your shoulders, elbows tucked close to your body.
Press through your hands to lift your chest off the ground, keeping your hips and legs on the floor.
Hold the position, feeling a stretch through the front of your torso, then lower back down.
coachNote: A gentle spinal extension pose that also opens the chest, useful after prolonged sitting or as a counter-stretch to flexion-heavy training.
tips: Keep the hips on the ground rather than pushing up into a full extension.
Keep the elbows slightly bent rather than fully locking out.
commonMistakes: Lifting the hips off the ground to force more height.
Fully locking out the elbows, straining the lower back.
benefits: Opens the chest and stretches the abdominal region.
Gentle counter to flexion-based sitting posture.
safetyNotes: Stop if you feel any sharp lower back pain.
Keep the movement gentle and controlled.
startingPosition: Lying face down, hands under the shoulders.
endingPosition: Chest lifted off the ground.

name: Child's Pose
instructions: Kneel on the floor, then sit your hips back toward your heels.
Fold your torso forward, extending your arms in front of you and resting your forehead on the ground.
Hold the position, breathing steadily and relaxing into the stretch.
coachNote: A restful, restorative pose commonly used to transition between more active yoga poses or simply to relieve tension at the end of a session.
tips: Widen the knees for more space if needed.
Breathe deeply and let your body relax into the position.
commonMistakes: Keeping the body tense instead of relaxing into the pose.
Forcing the hips all the way to the heels if flexibility limits it.
benefits: Provides a gentle, restful stretch for the back and hips.
Excellent for relieving general tension.
safetyNotes: Avoid if experiencing acute knee pain.
Use a cushion under the knees if needed.
startingPosition: Kneeling, about to sit back toward the heels.
endingPosition: Torso folded forward, arms extended, forehead on the ground.

name: Warrior I Pose
instructions: Step one foot back into a lunge stance, turning the back foot at a slight angle for stability.
Bend the front knee toward 90 degrees, squaring your hips forward, and raise both arms overhead.
Hold the position, feeling a stretch through the back leg's hip flexor, then switch sides.
coachNote: Combines a hip flexor stretch with balance and shoulder engagement, building both flexibility and stability simultaneously.
tips: Square the hips toward the front as much as possible.
Keep the front knee tracking over the ankle.
commonMistakes: Letting the front knee travel past the toes excessively.
Allowing the hips to remain angled instead of squaring forward.
benefits: Combines hip flexibility with balance and shoulder engagement.
Builds lower-body strength alongside mobility.
safetyNotes: Move into the position gradually.
Keep the front knee aligned with the foot to protect the joint.
startingPosition: Lunge stance, back foot angled.
endingPosition: Front knee bent to 90 degrees, arms raised overhead.

name: Warrior II Pose
instructions: Stand with feet wide apart, turning one foot out 90 degrees and the other slightly inward.
Bend the front knee toward 90 degrees, keeping your hips facing sideways, and extend both arms out at shoulder height.
Hold the position, gazing over the front hand, then switch sides.
coachNote: Builds hip opening and lower-body endurance while training shoulder stability in an extended, open position.
tips: Keep the front knee tracking directly over the ankle.
Keep the torso upright rather than leaning over the front leg.
commonMistakes: Leaning the torso forward over the front leg.
Letting the front knee cave inward.
benefits: Builds hip mobility and lower-body muscular endurance.
Trains shoulder stability in an open position.
safetyNotes: Move into the position gradually.
Keep the front knee aligned with the foot to protect the joint.
startingPosition: Wide stance, front foot turned out.
endingPosition: Front knee bent to 90 degrees, arms extended out to the sides.

name: Triangle Pose
instructions: Stand with feet wide apart, turning one foot out 90 degrees and the other slightly inward.
Extend your torso sideways over the front leg, reaching one hand toward your shin or the floor and the other arm toward the ceiling.
Hold the position, keeping both legs straight, then switch sides.
coachNote: A full side-body stretch that combines hamstring, adductor, and oblique flexibility with a rotational shoulder opening.
tips: Keep both legs straight throughout the pose.
Rotate the chest open toward the ceiling rather than facing the floor.
commonMistakes: Bending the front knee to reach further down.
Collapsing the chest toward the floor instead of rotating open.
benefits: Provides a comprehensive side-body and hamstring stretch.
Improves balance alongside flexibility.
safetyNotes: Move into the position gradually.
Use a block or support under the hand if needed.
startingPosition: Wide stance, front foot turned out.
endingPosition: Torso extended sideways over the front leg.

name: Seated Forward Fold
instructions: Sit on the floor with both legs extended straight in front of you.
Hinge forward at the hips, reaching toward your feet while keeping your back as flat as possible.
Hold the position, breathing steadily and relaxing further into the stretch as tolerated.
coachNote: A calming, restorative pose that stretches the entire posterior chain while promoting a relaxed, mindful state.
tips: Hinge from the hips rather than rounding the upper back excessively.
Use a strap around the feet if flexibility limits your reach.
commonMistakes: Forcing the stretch by rounding the back significantly.
Bouncing instead of holding a steady position.
benefits: Stretches the entire posterior chain.
Calming and restorative for the nervous system.
safetyNotes: Stretch to mild tension only.
Bend the knees slightly if the hamstrings are very tight.
startingPosition: Seated, legs extended straight.
endingPosition: Torso hinged forward over the legs.

name: Bridge Pose (Yoga)
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor close to your hips.
Press through your feet to lift your hips off the ground, interlacing your hands underneath you if comfortable.
Hold the position, feeling an opening through the chest and hip flexors, then lower back down.
coachNote: Unlike a strength-focused glute bridge, this yoga variation emphasizes holding a sustained extension to open the chest and hip flexors.
tips: Keep the knees tracking forward rather than splaying outward.
Press evenly through both feet.
commonMistakes: Overextending the neck by turning the head during the hold.
Letting the knees splay outward.
benefits: Opens the chest and hip flexors through sustained extension.
Gentle counter to flexion-based sitting posture.
safetyNotes: Keep the neck neutral, avoiding turning the head under load.
Stop if you feel any sharp lower back pain.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, knees bent, feet flat.
endingPosition: Hips lifted off the ground.

name: Thread the Needle
instructions: Start on hands and knees in a tabletop position.
Slide one arm underneath your body, reaching it across and resting your shoulder and ear on the ground.
Hold the position, feeling a stretch through the upper back and shoulder, then switch sides.
coachNote: A gentle way to stretch the posterior shoulder and thoracic spine, popularly used to relieve tension after upper-body training or overhead activity.
tips: Keep the hips square rather than rotating with the reaching arm.
Move into the position slowly and with control.
commonMistakes: Rotating the hips instead of keeping them stable.
Rushing into the position instead of easing in gradually.
benefits: Stretches the posterior shoulder and thoracic spine.
Calming, restorative stretch for the upper body.
safetyNotes: Move into the position gradually.
Use a cushion under the knees for comfort.
startingPosition: Tabletop position on hands and knees.
endingPosition: One arm threaded under the body, shoulder resting on the ground.

name: Reclining Spinal Twist
instructions: Lie on your back with arms extended out to the sides at shoulder height.
Bring one knee up and across your body, letting it fall toward the floor on the opposite side while keeping both shoulders grounded.
Hold the position, breathing steadily, then switch sides.
coachNote: A relaxing, restorative twist that's gentle on the spine, commonly used as a cool-down stretch at the end of a training session.
tips: Keep both shoulders pressed into the ground throughout.
Turn your head in the opposite direction of the twist for a fuller stretch if comfortable.
commonMistakes: Lifting the shoulder off the ground to let the knee drop further.
Forcing the knee down instead of letting gravity do the work.
benefits: Provides a gentle, relaxing spinal rotation stretch.
Excellent as a cool-down or end-of-day stretch.
safetyNotes: Move into the position gradually.
Avoid if experiencing acute lower back pain.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, arms extended to the sides.
endingPosition: One knee dropped across the body to the opposite side.

name: Shoulder Dislocates (Band/Stick)
instructions: Hold a mobility stick or light band with a wide overhand grip in front of your thighs.
Keeping your arms straight, raise the stick up and over your head, continuing the arc down behind your back.
Reverse the motion to bring the stick back to the starting position, and repeat for the desired reps.
coachNote: Named for how it takes the shoulder through an extreme range resembling a dislocation motion, this is a highly effective test and trainer of shoulder mobility.
tips: Use a wider grip if the shoulders are tight, narrowing it gradually as mobility improves.
Keep the arms as straight as comfortable throughout.
commonMistakes: Using a grip too narrow for current shoulder mobility, causing pain.
Rushing the movement instead of moving with control.
benefits: Effectively tests and improves shoulder flexibility.
Useful warm-up before overhead pressing or pulling.
safetyNotes: Use a wide enough grip to keep the movement pain-free.
Progress the grip width narrower only gradually over time.
startingPosition: Standing, stick held in front with a wide grip.
endingPosition: Stick brought behind the back, arms straight.

name: Hip CARs (Controlled Articular Rotations)
instructions: Stand tall, holding a support if needed, and brace your core to prevent your torso from moving.
Lift one knee up and slowly rotate it out to the side, around, and back, tracing the largest pain-free circle possible with the knee.
Move as slowly as possible to maximize control, then reverse direction and switch legs.
coachNote: Unlike passive stretching, CARs actively train the nervous system to control the full available range of a joint, which may help maintain or even expand mobility over time.
tips: Move as slowly as possible, prioritizing quality over speed.
Keep the torso completely still throughout the rotation.
commonMistakes: Moving too quickly, reducing the training effect.
Letting the torso rotate or lean to assist the movement.
benefits: Actively trains control through the hip's full range of motion.
May help maintain long-term joint health and mobility.
safetyNotes: Move only through a pain-free range.
Perform slowly and with full control.
startingPosition: Standing, one knee lifted.
endingPosition: Same position, knee traced through a full circle.

name: Shoulder CARs
instructions: Stand tall with one arm extended out to the side, bracing your core and ribcage to stay still.
Slowly rotate the arm through the largest pain-free circle possible, keeping the movement isolated to the shoulder joint.
Move as slowly as possible, then reverse direction and switch arms.
coachNote: A staple of joint health protocols, this slow and controlled circular motion helps maintain rotator cuff function and full shoulder range of motion.
tips: Move as slowly as possible, prioritizing quality over speed.
Keep the ribcage still, avoiding using the torso to cheat the range.
commonMistakes: Moving too quickly, reducing the training effect.
Letting the ribcage and torso move to assist the arm.
benefits: Actively trains control through the shoulder's full range of motion.
May help maintain long-term shoulder health.
safetyNotes: Move only through a pain-free range.
Perform slowly and with full control.
startingPosition: Standing, one arm extended to the side.
endingPosition: Same position, arm traced through a full circle.

name: Ankle CARs
instructions: Sit or stand and lift one foot slightly off the ground.
Slowly rotate your ankle through the largest pain-free circle possible, keeping the movement isolated to the ankle joint.
Move as slowly as possible, then reverse direction and switch feet.
coachNote: Improving ankle mobility and control can positively influence squat depth, running mechanics, and balance in general.
tips: Move as slowly as possible for maximum control.
Keep the movement isolated to the ankle, avoiding hip or knee compensation.
commonMistakes: Moving too quickly, reducing the training effect.
Using the knee or hip to fake the range of motion.
benefits: Improves ankle mobility, which supports squatting and running mechanics.
Quick and equipment-free.
safetyNotes: Move only through a pain-free range.
Perform slowly and with full control.
startingPosition: Seated or standing, one foot lifted slightly.
endingPosition: Same position, foot traced through a full circle.

name: Wrist CARs
instructions: Extend one arm in front of you, hand relaxed.
Slowly rotate your wrist through the largest pain-free circle possible, keeping the forearm still.
Move as slowly as possible, then reverse direction and switch hands.
coachNote: Important for lifters who place significant load through the wrists during pressing, pulling, and gripping exercises.
tips: Keep the forearm completely still, isolating the movement to the wrist.
Move as slowly as possible for maximum control.
commonMistakes: Moving the forearm or elbow to fake extra range.
Rushing through the movement.
benefits: Improves wrist mobility and control.
Quick warm-up before heavy pressing or gripping work.
safetyNotes: Move only through a pain-free range.
Perform slowly and with full control.
startingPosition: Arm extended, hand relaxed.
endingPosition: Same position, hand traced through a full circle.

name: Thoracic Spine Rotation (Open Book)
instructions: Lie on your side with your knees bent at 90 degrees and both arms extended in front of you, palms together.
Keeping your knees stacked and still, rotate your top arm up and across your body, following it with your gaze, letting your upper back rotate open toward the ceiling.
Return to the starting position with control, then repeat for the desired reps before switching sides.
coachNote: A key drill for improving thoracic rotation, which is frequently limited by desk posture and can affect throwing, swinging, and rotational athletic movements.
tips: Keep the knees stacked and stationary throughout.
Follow the moving hand with your eyes to encourage full rotation.
commonMistakes: Letting the knees and hips rotate along with the movement.
Moving too quickly instead of controlling each rotation.
benefits: Improves thoracic spine rotational mobility.
Beneficial for rotational sports and overhead movements.
safetyNotes: Move within a pain-free range.
Use a cushion under the head and knees for comfort.
startingPosition: Lying on the side, knees bent, arms extended together.
endingPosition: Top arm rotated across the body, upper back opened.

name: 90/90 Hip Switch
instructions: Sit on the floor in the 90/90 position, front leg bent in front, back leg bent behind you.
Lift both knees slightly and rotate your lower body to switch the leg positions, so the previously back leg is now in front.
Continue alternating sides in a controlled, flowing motion for the desired number of reps.
coachNote: A dynamic progression of the static 90/90 stretch, actively training rotational hip control and mobility rather than a passive hold.
tips: Move with control rather than using momentum to swing through.
Keep the torso as upright as possible throughout.
commonMistakes: Using the hands to push through the switch instead of the hips.
Rushing the movement, losing control of the transition.
benefits: Actively trains rotational hip mobility and control.
Useful for athletes in rotational or multi-directional sports.
safetyNotes: Move within a pain-free range.
Progress the speed and range of motion gradually.
startingPosition: Seated in the 90/90 position.
endingPosition: Legs switched to the opposite 90/90 position.

name: Deep Squat Hold (Baby Squat)
instructions: Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder width, toes turned out slightly.
Lower into the deepest comfortable squat position, keeping your heels on the ground.
Use your elbows to gently press your knees outward, and hold the position, breathing steadily.
coachNote: A foundational resting position in many cultures around the world, regularly practicing this hold can help restore natural hip, knee, and ankle mobility.
tips: Keep the heels flat on the ground throughout.
Use the elbows to encourage the knees to track outward.
commonMistakes: Letting the heels lift off the ground.
Rounding the back excessively instead of staying tall.
benefits: Restores natural hip, knee, and ankle mobility.
Simple, equipment-free daily mobility practice.
safetyNotes: Hold onto a support if balance is a concern.
Move within a pain-free range for the knees.
startingPosition: Standing, feet slightly wider than shoulder width.
endingPosition: Deep squat position held, heels down.

name: Ankle Dorsiflexion Stretch (Knee-to-Wall)
instructions: Kneel in a half-kneeling position with one foot flat on the ground close to a wall.
Keeping your heel down, drive your knee forward to gently tap the wall, then return.
Repeat for the desired reps, gradually moving the foot back as ankle mobility allows, then switch sides.
coachNote: A widely used assessment and improvement tool for ankle dorsiflexion, a key limiting factor in squat depth and running mechanics.
tips: Keep the heel flat on the ground throughout.
Move the foot further from the wall only as mobility genuinely improves.
commonMistakes: Letting the heel lift off the ground to reach the wall.
Progressing the foot position too quickly before earning the range.
benefits: Directly improves ankle dorsiflexion, aiding squat depth and running mechanics.
Simple to perform and track progress.
safetyNotes: Move within a pain-free range.
Progress gradually to avoid overloading the ankle.
startingPosition: Half-kneeling, front foot flat near a wall.
endingPosition: Knee driven forward toward the wall, heel down.

name: Cossack Squat Mobility Flow
instructions: Stand with feet wide apart, toes turned slightly outward.
Shift your weight to one side, bending that knee into a deep squat while keeping the opposite leg straight and foot flat.
Flow through the position and shift your weight to the other side, repeating continuously for the desired reps.
coachNote: A dynamic, flowing mobility drill that trains deep hip and adductor range under control, popular in athletic and functional training warm-ups.
tips: Keep both feet flat on the ground as much as possible.
Move with control rather than dropping quickly into each side.
commonMistakes: Letting the heel of the straight leg lift off the ground.
Rushing through the transition between sides.
benefits: Builds deep hip and adductor mobility under control.
Popular dynamic warm-up for athletic training.
safetyNotes: Progress the depth gradually as mobility allows.
Move within a pain-free range for the knees.
startingPosition: Standing, feet wide apart.
endingPosition: Weight shifted to one side, deep squat on that leg.

name: PNF Hamstring Stretch
instructions: Lie on your back and loop a strap around one foot, extending that leg toward the ceiling until you feel a mild stretch.
Gently push your leg against the strap's resistance for several seconds without moving, then relax and pull the leg slightly closer.
Repeat the contract-relax cycle for the desired number of rounds, then switch legs.
coachNote: Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation uses a contract-relax cycle that can produce greater short-term flexibility gains than static stretching alone.
tips: Use only a moderate contraction, not a maximal effort, against the strap.
Fully relax the muscle during the release phase before deepening the stretch.
commonMistakes: Contracting too hard, risking strain.
Not allowing full relaxation before pulling the leg further.
benefits: May produce greater short-term flexibility gains than static stretching alone.
Effective technique for stubborn tightness.
safetyNotes: Use a moderate, controlled contraction only.
Stop if you feel any sharp pain.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, strap looped around one foot, leg raised.
endingPosition: Leg pulled slightly closer after the contract-relax cycle.

name: Banded Hip Flexor Stretch
instructions: Loop a resistance band around a low anchor and step into it, positioning it high on the back thigh near the hip crease.
Step forward into a half-kneeling lunge position so the band pulls the hip gently backward.
Squeeze the glute of the back leg and shift your hips forward slightly to deepen the stretch, holding the position, then switch sides.
coachNote: The band's traction pulls the joint into a slight distraction, which can create a deeper and more effective hip flexor stretch than bodyweight versions alone.
tips: Squeeze the back glute to protect the lower back and deepen the true hip flexor stretch.
Set the band anchor at an appropriate height for a horizontal pull.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back excessively instead of squeezing the glute.
Using a band tension that's too aggressive for comfort.
benefits: Provides an enhanced hip flexor stretch through joint traction.
Effective for those with persistently tight hip flexors.
safetyNotes: Ensure the band anchor is secure before applying tension.
Progress the stretch depth gradually.
startingPosition: Half-kneeling, band anchored and positioned high on the back thigh.
endingPosition: Hips shifted forward, back glute squeezed.

name: Banded Shoulder Distraction Stretch
instructions: Loop a resistance band around a secure anchor at about shoulder height, and hold the other end with one hand.
Step or lean away from the anchor until there is tension pulling your arm and shoulder joint outward.
Gently move your arm through a comfortable range while the band maintains traction, holding briefly at end ranges, then switch sides.
coachNote: Uses light traction to create space in the shoulder joint, often used by lifters and throwers to relieve stiffness and improve range of motion.
tips: Use a light to moderate band tension, not maximal.
Move slowly and stop at any point that feels sharp or pinching.
commonMistakes: Using a band tension that's too aggressive.
Moving too quickly through the stretch instead of holding positions.
benefits: Creates joint traction that may relieve shoulder stiffness.
Popular recovery tool among throwing and lifting athletes.
safetyNotes: Ensure the band anchor is secure before applying tension.
Avoid if experiencing acute shoulder injury or instability.
startingPosition: Standing, band anchored, arm extended with tension.
endingPosition: Arm moved through a comfortable range under light traction.

name: Active Straight Leg Raise Stretch
instructions: Lie on your back with both legs extended flat on the floor.
Keeping the opposite leg pressed into the ground, actively raise one leg as high as possible without bending the knee, using only your own muscle strength.
Hold briefly near the top, then lower with control and repeat for the desired reps before switching legs.
coachNote: Unlike passive stretching using external assistance, this active method builds usable, functional flexibility by strengthening the hip flexors through the newly gained range.
tips: Keep the resting leg firmly pressed into the ground throughout.
Lift using active muscular effort rather than momentum.
commonMistakes: Letting the resting leg lift off the ground.
Bending the raised leg's knee to cheat additional height.
benefits: Builds functional, usable flexibility rather than passive range alone.
Strengthens the hip flexors through a newly gained range.
safetyNotes: Move within a pain-free range.
Keep the lower back flat against the floor throughout.
startingPosition: Lying on the back, both legs extended.
endingPosition: One leg raised as high as possible, knee straight.

name: Band-Assisted Overhead Shoulder Stretch
instructions: Hold a resistance band with a wide grip in front of your thighs.
Keeping your arms straight, raise the band overhead and gently press it backward as far as comfortable.
Hold the stretch at your end range, feeling it through the shoulders and lats, then return to the starting position.
coachNote: The band's slight elasticity provides a gentle overpressure at the end range, making this an accessible way to work on overhead shoulder flexibility.
tips: Use a wide enough grip to keep the stretch comfortable.
Keep the arms as straight as possible throughout.
commonMistakes: Using a grip too narrow, causing shoulder pain.
Arching the lower back to compensate for limited shoulder range.
benefits: Provides gentle overpressure for improving overhead shoulder flexibility.
Simple, accessible tool for shoulder mobility work.
safetyNotes: Use a wide enough grip to avoid pain.
Avoid if experiencing acute shoulder pain.
startingPosition: Standing, band held in front with a wide grip.
endingPosition: Band raised overhead and pressed backward.
